# Souppaya, Scarfone and Dodson, Secure Software Development Framework v1.1

**Source:** Murugiah Souppaya, Karen Scarfone and Donna Dodson (2022), *Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1: Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities*. NIST Special Publication 800-218, February 2022. DOI: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218. Licence: United States public domain; worldwide reprint and derivative-work permission under NIST Technical Series Publications policy. Republished courtesy of the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
**Scope:** open
**Structure:** Covers and Authority (PDF pp. 1–3); Reports on Computer Systems Technology, Abstract, Keywords and Trademark Information (printed p. ii); Acknowledgments and Audience (pp. iii–iv); Note to Readers (p. iv); Patent Disclosure Notice (p. v); Executive Summary (p. vi); Table of Contents and List of Tables (p. vii); 1 Introduction (pp. 1–3); 2 The Secure Software Development Framework (pp. 4–19, including all of Table 1); References (pp. 20–23); Appendix A—The SSDF and Executive Order 14028 (p. 24, Table 2); Appendix B—Acronyms (pp. 25–26); Appendix C—Change Log (p. 27).
**Citation style:** `(§1, p. 3)` and `(Table 1, PO.3.2, p. 7)` use the source's printed page numbers. Printed page 1 is PDF page 10. Front matter uses Roman numbering or a PDF-page anchor.
**Coverage:** Full text of all 36 PDF pages read, including every task, notional example, reference mapping, footnote, bibliography entry and appendix. Full image scope: every page inspected for visual content; Table 1's 15 page panels and Table 2 retained as 16 substantive images. Three extracted appendix-label bitmaps are typography, classified decorative; their labels are restored as navigation in the converted text. No substantive diagram is omitted.

## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

Secure software development practices should be integrated throughout an organisation's existing software development life cycle (SDLC), because few SDLC models explicitly address software security in detail. The authors argue that doing so should reduce the number of vulnerabilities in released software, reduce the potential impact of exploiting undetected or unaddressed vulnerabilities, and address the root causes of vulnerabilities to prevent recurrences. The framework is a set of high-level practices drawn from existing standards and guidance; it does not introduce new practices or terminology. [AR] (Abstract, p. ii; Executive Summary, p. vi; §1, p. 1)

The SSDF specifies outcomes while leaving implementation methods to organisations. Its common vocabulary supports conversations within producer organisations and between producers and acquirers. The recommendations recognise that each producer may have unique security assumptions and each acquirer unique security needs and requirements; implementation should be tailored using risk, cost, feasibility, applicability and automatability. The practices and examples are a starting point, not a prioritised checklist or prescribed implementation sequence. [AR] (Executive Summary, p. vi; §1, pp. 2–3; §2, p. 4)

## Part I: Purpose, audience and interpretation

### Front-matter limits and audience

The Authority statement identifies NIST's statutory responsibilities, says this guideline does not supersede existing federal authorities or mandatory standards, and permits voluntary use by nongovernmental organisations. Mention of a commercial entity does not imply NIST endorsement or that it is the best available option. [AP] (Authority, PDF p. 3)

The primary audiences are software producers of any size, sector or maturity and software acquirers, including federal agencies. Readers do not need secure-development expertise to understand the document, but the text explicitly says such expertise is needed to implement its recommended practices. The Audience section also identifies relevant NICE workforce categories: Securely Provision, Operate and Maintain, Oversee and Govern, Protect and Defend, and Analyze. [AP] [BT] (Audience, pp. iii–iv)

The Acknowledgments describe a June 2021 workshop and more than 150 position papers contributing to this update, together with public comments from dozens of organisations and individuals. The Note to Readers invites continuing feedback and points standards organisations towards the National Online Informative References Program for mappings. The Patent Disclosure Notice reports no patent claims identified to ITL by publication, while explicitly declining to imply that licences are unnecessary; ITL had not undertaken a patent search. [AP] (Acknowledgments, p. iii; Note to Readers, p. iv; Patent Disclosure Notice, p. v)

### Integrate security throughout the life cycle

The publication uses SDLC to mean software, not system, development life cycle; software includes code built into hardware. Its examples of life-cycle models include waterfall, spiral, agile and agile combined with DevOps. Vulnerabilities include coding flaws and weaknesses from configuration, incorrect trust assumptions and outdated risk analysis. The latter breadth is attributed to NIST IR 7864. [AP] [BT] (§1, p. 1 and footnote 1)

Addressing security earlier generally requires less eventual effort and cost for the same security level. The source calls this shifting left and argues that it reduces technical debt from having to remedy early flaws late in development or production; it can also improve security and resilience. [AR] (§1, p. 1)

The high-level form allows use across sectors, organisation sizes, technologies and workflows, including IT, industrial control systems, cyber-physical systems and the Internet of Things. The authors describe uses in documenting current practices, setting future targets, continuous improvement, moving practices to modern development models, and understanding suppliers' practices. [AP] (§1, p. 2)

> "The focus is on the outcomes of the practices rather than on the tools, techniques, and mechanisms to do so."
>
> [V] (Executive Summary, p. vi)

### Tailoring, shared responsibility and non-prescription

All applicable practices are the aim, but the extent and formality of implementation vary with a producer's security assumptions. Some practices are foundational and others depend on those foundations. A compiler-related practice is unnecessary for software that uses no compiler. Frequencies in examples are notional, and the practices are not all equally important in every situation. [AP] (§1, p. 3)

Where software delivery uses platform or service providers, responsibility can be distributed. The source describes a likely shared-responsibility model and says the tenant should agree with providers who owns each practice and task, and how providers attest to conformance. [AP] (§1, p. 3)

> "The intention of the SSDF is not to create a checklist to follow, but to provide a basis for planning and implementing a risk-based approach to adopting secure software development practices."
>
> [V] (§1, p. 3)

### How to read the framework and Table 1

Four groups organise the practices: Prepare the Organization (PO), Protect the Software (PS), Produce Well-Secured Software (PW), and Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV). They respectively concern organisational readiness; protection from tampering and unauthorised access; secure software production; and identifying, addressing and preventing recurrence of residual vulnerabilities. [AP] (§2, p. 4)

Each practice has an identifier and explanation, tasks, notional implementation examples, and mappings to established secure-development references. Neither a particular example nor any combination of examples is required; other implementations are possible. The table is a space-constrained subset of what an organisation may need, and its order implies neither priority nor sequence. The publication does not define terms such as sensitive data, qualified person and well-secured; adopters should define them in their own context, and likewise the names of environments such as development, build, staging, integration, test, production and distribution. Enumerating environments is necessary to secure them properly, especially to prevent attackers' lateral movement between environments. [AP] (§2, p. 4)

## Part II: Prepare the Organization (PO)

### PO.1—Define Security Requirements for Software Development

PO.1 calls for requirements to be known throughout the SDLC, including internal policies, objectives and risk strategy and external laws or regulations. Collecting requirements once and sharing them minimises duplicated effort. [AP] (Table 1, PO.1, p. 5)

| Task | Requirement and source's notional examples |
|---|---|
| PO.1.1 | Identify, document and maintain requirements for development infrastructure and processes. Examples cover infrastructure/endpoints, development processes and third-party components; reviewing requirements at least annually or after relevant changes/incidents; and educating affected people. [AP] [AE] (p. 5) |
| PO.1.2 | Identify, document and maintain the organisation's software security requirements. Examples include architecture/design policies, security gates and vulnerability responses, technology-stack risk, release retention, support/end-of-life notices, regular or event-driven review, and periodically reviewing approved exceptions. [AP] [AE] (p. 5) |
| PO.1.3 | Communicate requirements to third parties supplying commercial components for reuse. Examples put core requirements into contracts/acquisition documents, define supplier selection criteria, require compliance attestations and provenance/integrity mechanisms, and manage and review exceptions for unmet requirements. This task was formerly PW.3.1. [AP] [AE] (pp. 5–6) |

The provenance footnote borrows from SP 800-53: it is the chronology of the origin, development, ownership, location and changes to a system or component and associated data, and may also include the personnel and processes that interact with or modify them. [BT] (Table 1, footnote 5, p. 6)

### PO.2—Implement Roles and Responsibilities

Everyone involved in the SDLC, inside or outside the organisation, should be prepared for their assigned responsibilities. PO.2.1 creates or alters roles to encompass all SDLC parts and maintains them. Examples include integrating security roles with development, naming code owners, communicating changes and using tools for engagement. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.2.1, p. 6)

PO.2.2 provides role-based training and periodically reviews proficiency and training. Examples specify desired outcomes, curricula and role-specific plans, acquiring or creating suitable training and measuring outcome performance to improve it. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.2.2, p. 6)

PO.2.3 obtains and communicates upper-management or authorising-official commitment. Examples include appointing one leader or a leadership team accountable for the entire secure-development process, including production release and delegation, and educating leaders and personnel about the risks and commitment. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.2.3, p. 7)

### PO.3—Implement Supporting Toolchains

Automation is intended to reduce human effort and improve accuracy, reproducibility, usability and comprehensiveness while documenting that practices were performed. Toolchains may operate at organisation, project or life-cycle-stage level. [AP] (Table 1, PO.3, p. 7)

| Task | Requirement and source's notional examples |
|---|---|
| PO.3.1 | Specify required/recommended tools and their integration to mitigate identified risk. Examples classify toolchains, integrate security tools, define exchanged information/formats, evaluate tools' signing capabilities for creating immutable, auditable records/logs and automate orchestration. [AP] [AE] (p. 7) |
| PO.3.2 | Securely deploy, operate and maintain tools/toolchains. Examples include tool security assessment, workflow integration, configuration as code, reproducible builds, upgrades, monitoring logs, provenance/integrity verification, and links to PW.6 and PO.5. [AP] [AE] (p. 7) |
| PO.3.3 | Configure tools to generate artefacts showing support for the organisation's practices. Examples use workflow/issue tools for audit trails, set audit frequency and security/retention policies, and assign responsibility for evidence tools cannot generate. [AP] [AE] (pp. 7–8) |

The artefact footnote adapts IR 7692's definition as a piece of evidence, uses SP 800-160's definition of evidence, and says these artefacts record secure-development practices. [BT] (Table 1, footnote 6, p. 7)

### PO.4—Define and Use Criteria for Software Security Checks

PO.4.1 defines and tracks security-check criteria across the SDLC. Examples assess how effectively risk is managed, use KPIs/KRIs/severity measures, add security to the Definition of Done, assess workflow evidence, record approvals/rejections/exception requests, and learn from project successes and failures. PO.4.2 gathers and safeguards supporting information; examples automate gathering and criteria-based decision-making, periodically review those decision-making processes, add tools where necessary, and restrict access while preventing alteration/deletion. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.4.1–PO.4.2, p. 8)

### PO.5—Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development

PO.5.1 separates and protects development environments. Examples include multifactor/risk-based authentication, conditional access, network segmentation and access controls, restricted ingress/egress, minimised direct human access to toolchains and minimised use of production software/services from non-production environments, auditing trust relationships/privilege use, monitoring and incident handling, control-generated artefacts, vulnerability monitoring, and zero-trust hosting; the zero-trust hosting example's footnote directs readers to SP 800-207. [AP] [AE] [BT] (Table 1, PO.5.1 and footnote 7, pp. 8–9)

PO.5.2 secures and hardens development endpoints using a risk-based approach. Examples include approved hardening guides, encryption, least functionality and privilege, posture/privileged-access monitoring, evidence generation, multifactor authentication, dedicated non-production development endpoints separate from endpoints for other tasks, and zero-trust configuration. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.5.2, p. 9)

## Part III: Protect the Software (PS)

### PS.1—Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering

PS.1 seeks to prevent accidental or intentional unauthorised changes that undermine intended security. PS.1.1 stores source, executable and configuration-as-code using least privilege. Examples include repositories with protection appropriate to public versus confidential code, account-attributed version history, commit signing, code-owner approval of others' changes, executable signing and cryptographic hashes. The code-signing footnote points to NIST's *Security Considerations for Code Signing*. [AP] [AE] [BT] (Table 1, PS.1.1 and footnote 8, p. 9)

### PS.2—Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity

PS.2.1 makes integrity-verification information available to acquirers, helping them establish that software is legitimate and untampered. Examples publish release hashes on a secured website, use certificate-authority-backed code signing so consumer tools can check signatures, and review signing processes including renewal, rotation, revocation and protection. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PS.2.1, p. 10)

### PS.3—Archive and Protect Each Software Release

PS.3.1 securely archives required release files and supporting integrity/provenance data to support later vulnerability work. Examples limit repositories to necessary read-only access and separately protect or sign supporting data. PS.3.2 collects, protects, maintains and shares provenance for every release component, for example in an SBOM. Examples share it with acquirers according to policy, preferably using standard formats, and with operations/response teams; let recipients verify integrity; and update provenance whenever components change. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PS.3.1–PS.3.2, p. 10)

## Part IV: Produce Well-Secured Software (PW)

### PW.1—Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks

PW.1 identifies requirements, operational security risks and architectural/design mitigations, and justifies risk-based exceptions. PW.1.1 uses risk modelling, such as threat modelling, attack modelling or attack-surface mapping. Examples train teams or involve experts, concentrate rigorous assessment on high-risk areas, use earlier vulnerability reports and classify data. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.1–PW.1.1, p. 11)

PW.1.2 tracks requirements, risks and design decisions. Examples record risk responses, mitigation plans and exception rationales, carry mitigations into requirements, retain records for audit/maintenance and periodically reconsider exceptions. PW.1.3 supports standard security services/features where appropriate rather than proprietary implementations; examples include repositories of modules, secure reusable configurations, and criteria for features that developed software must support. The task was formerly PW.4.3. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.1.2–PW.1.3, p. 11)

### PW.2—Review the Software Design to Verify Compliance with Security Requirements and Risk Information

PW.2.1 calls for review by qualified people who did not design the software and/or automated toolchain processes, to check requirements and identified risks. Examples review the design and risk models, correct failures, change the design or risk-response strategy when necessary, and record findings in specifications, issue trackers or threat models. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.2.1, p. 12)

### PW.3—Retired identifier

Table 1 marks PW.3 as moved into PW.4, PW.3.1 as moved to PO.1.3 and PW.3.2 as moved to PW.4.4. These unshaded rows preserve identifier history rather than add live practices. [AP] (Table 1, p. 12; Appendix C, p. 27)

### PW.4—Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible Instead of Duplicating Functionality

The authors argue that reusing components with checked security posture can lower cost, speed development and reduce newly introduced vulnerabilities, especially for security functionality such as cryptography. [AR] (Table 1, PW.4, p. 12)

| Task | Requirement and source's notional examples |
|---|---|
| PW.4.1 | Acquire and maintain well-secured third-party components. Examples assess expected use and reassess changed use, publish secure configurations, analyse provenance, host vetted open-source components, maintain approved versions, designate required components, manage upgrades while retaining older versions during transition, and build binaries from verified source when acquired binary integrity/provenance cannot be confirmed. [AP] [AE] (p. 12) |
| PW.4.2 | Create/maintain well-secured in-house components for common needs not better met externally. Examples apply organisational SDLC practices, provide secure configurations and repositories, designate required components and manage version transitions. [AP] [AE] (p. 12) |
| PW.4.4 | Verify third-party components against organisational requirements throughout their life cycles. Examples check known vulnerabilities automatically, use vetting services, confirm ongoing maintenance, plan for end-of-life/unavailable components, verify integrity and review/analyse/test code. [AP] [AE] (p. 13) |

Table 1 marks PW.4.3 as moved to PW.1.3 and PW.4.5 as moved to PW.4.1 and PW.4.4. The final-version change log describes deleting PW.4.5 as a merge into PW.4.4; both statements are retained as their source locations present them. [AP] (Table 1, pp. 12–13; Appendix C, p. 27)

### PW.5—Create Source Code by Adhering to Secure Coding Practices

PW.5.1 follows coding practices appropriate to languages/environments and requirements. Examples validate input/output and encode output, avoid unsafe functions, handle errors, enable logging/tracing, support secure coding with development-tool training, use manual checks when automation is insufficient, apply linters/formatters, check common vulnerabilities and have developers review their own code to complement other people/tools. PW.5.2 is retired into an example under PW.5.1. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.5.1–PW.5.2, p. 13)

### PW.6—Configure the Compilation, Interpreter, and Build Processes to Improve Executable Security

PW.6.1 selects compiler/interpreter/build tools with security-improving features. Examples keep them current, use change management, audit unexpected changes and validate authenticity/integrity. PW.6.2 selects, implements and uses approved security configurations. Examples enable warnings, treat them as errors except identified false positives/irrelevancies, use controlled build environments, enable execution randomisation/obfuscation, test the features, continuously verify approved settings and distribute configuration as code. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.6.1–PW.6.2, p. 14)

### PW.7—Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements

PW.7.1 selects human review and/or tool-based analysis according to policy and software stage, potentially including third-party and reusable code. PW.7.2 performs review/analysis against coding standards and records/triages findings and remediation recommendations in team workflows. Examples include peer reviews, experts looking for malicious code/backdoors, documented review discussion, static analysis with human handling of findings, checklists, continuous detection/remediation of verified unsafe practices, root-cause records and searchable lessons. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.7.1–PW.7.2, pp. 14–15)

### PW.8—Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements

Executable code includes binaries, directly executed bytecode/source, and other code the organisation treats as executable. PW.8.1 decides whether testing is needed to discover vulnerabilities missed earlier and selects types according to policy and software stage. PW.8.2 scopes, designs, runs and documents tests and records/triages issues/remediations. [AP] (Table 1, PW.8.1–PW.8.2, p. 15)

The notional tests include security-feature functional testing, dynamic vulnerability tests in automated suites, regression tests for earlier vulnerabilities, production infrastructure/stack considerations, fuzzing, and penetration testing for high-risk scenarios if resources permit. Examples also record root causes and searchable lessons and draw on code/design records when planning tests. [AE] (Table 1, PW.8.2, p. 15)

### PW.9—Configure Software to Have Secure Settings by Default

PW.9.1 determines a secure default baseline that does not weaken the security supplied by the platform, network or services; its example tests security and operational effects of settings. PW.9.2 implements and documents defaults. Examples verify approved configuration, document purpose/options/defaults/security relevance/operational impact/relationships with other settings, provide programmatic implementation/assessment mechanisms and use change control for configuration. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.9.1–PW.9.2, p. 16)

## Part V: Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV)

### RV.1—Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis

RV.1.1 gathers possible vulnerability reports from acquirers, users and public sources and investigates credible reports, including third-party components. Examples monitor databases/mailing lists, use threat intelligence and automatically revisit provenance/composition data. RV.1.2 reviews, analyses or tests code for undetected vulnerabilities; its examples run automated analysis/testing regularly or continuously for all supported releases and refer to PW.7 and PW.8. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, RV.1.1–RV.1.2, pp. 16–17)

RV.1.3 establishes disclosure/remediation policy and supporting responsibilities/processes. Examples create an accessible disclosure programme, establish a PSIRT with stakeholder communication plans, prepare playbooks for ordinary reports, zero-days, exploitation and multiparty incidents, and exercise response processes periodically. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, RV.1.3, p. 17)

### RV.2—Assess, Prioritize, and Remediate Vulnerabilities

RV.2.1 gathers enough risk information to plan remediation or another response. Examples record vulnerabilities in an issue tracker and calculate risk using exploitability, potential impact and other relevant characteristics. RV.2.2 plans and implements responses. Examples make risk-based remediation/acceptance/transference decisions, prioritise actions, plan temporary mitigation when a permanent fix is unavailable, publish actionable advisories, deliver remediation through trusted automated mechanisms and update design/risk/exception records. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, RV.2.1–RV.2.2, pp. 17–18)

### RV.3—Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes

RV.3.1 identifies root causes of vulnerabilities, with examples recording causes and lessons in a searchable developer wiki. RV.3.2 analyses causes over time for patterns; examples also add automated toolchain detections and update manual processes. RV.3.3 proactively finds and fixes similar vulnerabilities to eradicate a class rather than waiting for outside reports, referring to PW.7/PW.8. RV.3.4 reviews and updates the SDLC to reduce recurrence in updates and new software, with examples capturing lessons and implementing changed practices. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, RV.3.1–RV.3.4, pp. 18–19)

## Part VI: Appendices, references and visual structure

### Appendix A—The SSDF and Executive Order 14028

The appendix links the work to EO 14028's software-supply-chain initiatives and NIST's direction to solicit input and identify/develop guidance. Table 2 maps every listed Section 4e subsection to SSDF practices/tasks that can help address it using a risk-based approach. For example, 4e(vii) maps to PS.3.2; 4e(viii) maps to RV.1.1, RV.1.2, RV.1.3, RV.2.1, RV.2.2 and RV.3.3; and 4e(ix) maps to all practices and tasks consistent with a risk-based approach. It points to separately published communication guidance for conformance attestation. [AP] [BT] (Appendix A, Table 2, p. 24)

### Appendix B—Acronyms

The appendix defines selected acronyms and abbreviations used in the publication, including SDLC as Software Development Life Cycle, SBOM as Software Bill of Materials, PSIRT as Product Security Incident Response Team, KPI as Key Performance Indicator and KRI as Key Risk Indicator. It also expands several organisation and standard names that appear within the reference-mapping labels, such as BSIMM, CNCF, IEC, ISO, NTIA, OWASP and PCI; the mapping labels themselves are keyed in the References list. [AP] (Appendix B, pp. 25–26; References, pp. 20–23)

### Appendix C—Change Log

The appendix distinguishes the February 2022 final changes from the September 2021 draft changes relative to the April 2020 SSDF. The final changes include deleting/merging PW.4.5, adding numerous public-comment examples and example numbers, adding/updating references, wording edits and definitions of provenance, artefact and evidence. Draft changes include adding PO.5; removing PW.3 into PW.4; adding PO.1.2, PO.5.1, PO.5.2, PS.3.2 and PW.1.2; moving several tasks; demoting PW.5.2 to an example; updating references; retiring moved/deleted identifiers; colour/shading conventions; conversion from white paper to SP 800 series; and adding Appendix A. [AP] (Appendix C, p. 27)

### Tables and figures

Table 1 occupies printed pp. 5–19. It uses four columns—practices, tasks, notional implementation examples and references—with group borders and shaded live-practice rows. Unshaded moved/retired rows preserve the old identifiers. Table 2 on p. 24 is a two-column EO-subsection-to-SSDF mapping. There are no separate numbered figures in the publication's List of Tables/contents. [AP] (List of Tables, p. vii; Table 1, pp. 5–19; Table 2, p. 24; Appendix C, p. 27)

| Metric | Value | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| Framework groups | Four: PO, PS, PW, RV | [AP] (§2, p. 4) |
| Position papers NIST received in response to EO 14028 §4, alongside a June 2021 workshop | More than 150 | [AP] (Acknowledgments, p. iii) |

## Connections the author makes in the text

- **NIST Cybersecurity Framework v1.1:** an analogy for providing a common language. The footnote says SSDF practices may support CSF outcomes but do not map to its Functions/Categories/Subcategories and are typically different parties' responsibility. [BT] (§1, p. 2 and footnote 2)
- **NIST IR 7864:** cited for the breadth of vulnerability types beyond coding flaws. **SP 800-53**, **IR 7692** and **SP 800-160** supply the provenance/artefact/evidence definitions. **SP 800-207** and the NIST code-signing white paper are footnote pointers for zero trust and code signing. [BT] (§1, p. 1; Table 1, footnotes 5–8, pp. 6–9)
- **Mapped secure-development guidance:** the bibliography and Table 1 include BSA Framework for Secure Software v1.1; BSIMM12; CNCF *Software Supply Chain Best Practices*; IDA SOAR; IEC 62443-4-1; ISO/IEC 27034-1, 29147 and 30111; Microsoft SDL; PCI Secure SLC v1.1; and SAFECode guides on agile security tasks, fundamental practices, software integrity, third-party components and tactical threat modelling. These are reference mappings, not independently re-ingested evidence here. [BT] (Table 1; References, pp. 20–23)
- **OWASP:** Table 1 maps to ASVS 4.0.3, MASVS 1.4.2, SAMM 1.5 and SCVS 1.0 as listed in this 2022 bibliography. These mappings are to those editions. [BT] (References, p. 21)
- **Additional NIST and government references:** IR 8397 developer verification; NIST consumer-software labelling criteria; NTIA minimum SBOM elements; SP 800-53 Rev. 5; SP 800-160 Vol. 1; the second draft of SP 800-161 Rev. 1; SP 800-181 NICE; draft SP 800-216 vulnerability-disclosure guidelines; and EO 14028. Table 1/Appendix A use these as mapped references or supporting context. [BT] (References, pp. 20–23; Appendix A, p. 24)
- **Getting-started pointers:** the Introduction's footnote 4 directs readers to Steve Lipner's *SDL That Won't Break the Bank*, Lipner and Stacy Simpson's *Application Software Security and the CIS Controls*, and Microsoft's *Simplified Implementation of the Microsoft SDL*. [BT] (§1, p. 3, footnote 4)

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- **A uniform checklist or prescribed sequence:** the source explicitly rejects a checklist intention and says practices/examples are neither prioritised nor implementation-ordered; it also states that no example or combination of examples is required and that the examples are not the only feasible options. Risk and context govern selection and implementation. [AP] (§1, p. 3; §2, p. 4)
